e.etymology: The feminine form of Ciarán, from Irish ciar, dark or black-haired. A 7th-century Irish saint bore the name, and it is often anglicized as Keira or Kiera.
namesakes: Ciara (R&B singer of Goodies and 1, 2 Step)

assoc.t: R&B singer Ciara, known by her first name
Revlon's Ciara perfume

e.note: Irish speakers say KEER-uh; many Americans say see-AIR-uh, as the singer does, so expect to correct people.

e.etymology: Usually explained as a Swahili name meaning mighty. It came into American use in the 1970s among Black families choosing African names.
namesakes: Jelani Cobb (New Yorker writer and Columbia journalism dean)

e.etymology: An anglicized spelling of Irish Aisling, the word for a dream or vision and the name of a genre of Irish poetry in which Ireland appears as a woman. It became a given name in the 20th century.
e.note: The Irish pronunciation is ASH-ling or ASH-lin; many Americans read the spelling as AYZ-lin.

e.etymology: A short form of Italian names such as Giovanni (John), Giorgio (George) and Giuseppe (Joseph), now also given on its own. In Georgia it is short for Giorgi.
namesakes: Gio Reyna (US national team soccer player)
Gio Gonzalez (two-time All-Star MLB pitcher)

assoc.t: Armani's Acqua di Gio fragrance

e.etymology: From Hebrew Shimon, hearkening or listening, the name of a son of Jacob and of the old man who blessed the infant Jesus in the Temple. Simon is the same name in its Greek-shaped form.
namesakes: Simeon Rice (Super Bowl-winning NFL defensive end)

e.etymology: The French and German form of Emily, from Latin Aemilia, the feminine of the Roman family name Aemilius, traditionally linked to aemulus, rival.
namesakes: Emilie de Ravin (actress in Lost and Once Upon a Time)

e.etymology: A modern American girls' name with no settled source, close in sound to Zara, Maya and Zoya. Zaya is also an Assyrian man's name and surname.
namesakes: Zaya Wade (model, daughter of Dwyane Wade)

e.etymology: From Sanskrit lila, play, the Hindu idea that the world is the playful creative act of the divine. Leela is the usual English spelling in India; Lila is the same name.
namesakes: Leela (the one-eyed starship captain in Futurama)

assoc.t: Leela, the one-eyed captain in Futurama

e.etymology: From the capital of Kenya, named for the Maasai phrase Enkare Nairobi, cool water, after the river that runs through it. It joined American place names like Kenya and Asia as a girls' name.

assoc.t: capital city of Kenya
Nairobi, a robber in Netflix's Money Heist

e.etymology: Arabic inara means illumination or lighting. The same spelling is a Latvian name of uncertain origin and the name of a Hittite goddess of wild animals.
namesakes: Inara Serra (companion aboard Serenity in the TV series Firefly)

assoc.t: Inara Serra in the TV series Firefly

e.etymology: A modern American name that sets Bryn, from Welsh bryn, hill, on the -ley ending, or respells the English surname Brinley.
From the Irish name Cianán, a diminutive of Cian, ancient or enduring. It reached American use through the surname Keenan.
namesakes: Keenan Allen (NFL wide receiver)

e.etymology: Taken up as a given name after the 1994 film The Crow, whose hero is the murdered musician Eric Draven. The surname has no established meaning; it echoes the word raven.
namesakes: Eric Draven (hero of the 1994 film The Crow)

assoc.t: Eric Draven, the avenging hero of The Crow
Draven, an axe-throwing champion in League of Legends

e.etymology: A feminine form of Ariel, from Hebrew ari, lion, and el, God. In the Bible Ariel is a poetic name for Jerusalem.
A modern American respelling of Kason, itself a recent name that rhymes with Mason and Jason and echoes the English surname Cason.
A 20th-century American coinage that joins Kay or Kayla to the -lyn ending, one of many spellings of Kaylyn.
A respelling of Jacoby, a surname built on Jacob, that folds in the name Kobe. Its use peaked in 2020, the year Kobe Bryant died.
A respelling of Cruz, the Spanish word for cross and a common Hispanic surname, long given in honor of the Holy Cross.

assoc.t: sounds the same as the word cruise

e.etymology: From Latin Iuppiter, sky father, the king of the Roman gods and the planet named for him. Its recent use for girls follows the rise of the similar-sounding Juniper.

assoc.t: the largest planet in the solar system
king of the gods in Roman mythology
Jupiter, a beach town in Florida

e.etymology: Used mostly as a dressed-up spelling of the word rain. Raine is also an English surname drawn from old Germanic names such as Raymond, and a Finnish men's name.
e.note: Sounds the same as rain, reign and rein, so the spelling will often need to be given.

e.etymology: From Ya-Sin, the title of the 36th chapter of the Quran, which opens with the Arabic letters ya and sin. Their meaning is unknown, and tradition takes the phrase as a name of the Prophet Muhammad.
The English word, from Old English treowth, faithfulness. It follows virtue names such as Faith and Justice into modern use.
namesakes: Sojourner Truth (abolitionist and women's rights speaker)

assoc.t: abolitionist Sojourner Truth, who chose the surname
truth, the national anti-smoking campaign

e.etymology: An old spelling of Gaius, one of the commonest Roman first names, borne by Julius Caesar. Its meaning is uncertain; an old tradition links it to Latin gaudere, to rejoice.
e.note: Readers split between KY-us and KAY-us; the Cambridge college of the same name is said like keys.

e.etymology: An English occupational surname for the bailiff who ran a grange, an outlying farm or granary, from Old French grangier.
namesakes: Granger Smith (country singer)
Hermione Granger (heroine of the Harry Potter series)

assoc.t: Hermione Granger's surname in Harry Potter

e.etymology: A short form of William, from the Germanic elements wil, will or desire, and helm, helmet or protection. It has also long been given as a full name in its own right.
namesakes: Will Smith (actor)
Will Ferrell (comedian and actor)
Will Rogers (humorist)

assoc.t: the everyday word will, as in willpower or a last will
Will Byers in Stranger Things

e.etymology: A pet form of Leonard, from Old High German leo, lion, and hart, hard or brave. It is now given to girls as well as boys.
namesakes: Lenny Kravitz (rock musician)
Lenny Bruce (stand-up comedian)

assoc.t: Lenny Kravitz, rock musician
Lenny Leonard, Homer's coworker on The Simpsons

e.etymology: The king of the Greek gods, ruler of sky and thunder. The name comes from an ancient root meaning sky or daylight, the same one behind Latin Jove and deus, god.

assoc.t: king of the Greek gods, wielder of thunderbolts
a stock name for large dogs

e.note: A common name for big dogs, and one that carries the full weight of the Greek god.

e.meaning: son of the servant of Saint John
e.etymology: From a surname that goes back to Gaelic Mac Gille Eoin, son of the servant of Saint John, the same root as MacLean. Its use as a first name is recent.
namesakes: Macklin Celebrini (first pick in the 2024 NHL draft)

e.etymology: The Spanish and Italian name for the French region of Lorraine, often linked by sound to Laura. In the US it spread with the 1857 ballad Lorena, a favorite of Civil War soldiers.
namesakes: Lorena Ochoa (Mexican golfer, former world number one)
Lorena Bobbitt (figure in a notorious 1993 assault case)
e.note: Americans who remember the 1990s may think of Lorena Bobbitt, who made headlines for maiming her husband.

assoc.t: Lorena Bobbitt, of the notorious 1993 assault case

e.etymology: An English surname from places named in Old English with hreod, reeds, or rydde, cleared land, plus leah, a woodland clearing.
namesakes: Ridley Scott (director of Alien and Gladiator)
Daisy Ridley (actress who played Rey in Star Wars)

assoc.t: Ridley, the dragon villain of Nintendo's Metroid

e.etymology: In the US, a spelling of Amiyah, a modern name in the family of Amaya and Maya. Amiya is separately a Bengali name from the Sanskrit word for nectar.
e.note: People will split between uh-MY-uh and uh-MEE-uh on sight.

e.etymology: A spelling of Niko or Nico, short forms of Nicholas, from Greek nike, victory, and laos, people. Nikko is also a Japanese city of shrines whose name means sunlight.

assoc.t: Nikko, a shrine city and national park in Japan
